Abstract
Large Language Models (LLMs) are increas-
ingly deployed in persona-driven applications
such as education, customer service, and social
platforms, where models are prompted to adopt
specific personas when interacting with users.
While persona conditioning can improve user
experience and engagement, it also raises con-
cerns about how personality cues may interact
with gender biases and stereotypes.
In this
work, we present a controlled study of persona-
conditioned story generation in English and
Hindi, where each story portrays a working pro-
fessional in India producing context-specific
artifacts (e.g., lesson plans, reports, letters)
under systematically varied persona gender, oc-
cupational role, and personality traits from the
HEXACO and Dark Triad frameworks. Across
23, 400 generated stories from six state-of-the-
art LLMs, we find that personality traits are
significantly associated with both the magni-
tude and direction of gender bias. In particular,
Dark Triad personality traits are consistently
associated with higher gender-stereotypical
representations compared to socially desirable
HEXACO traits, though these associations
vary across models and languages. Our find-
ings demonstrate that gender bias in LLMs
is not static but context-dependent.
This
suggests that persona-conditioned systems
used in real-world applications may introduce
uneven representational harms,
reinforcing
gender stereotypes in generated educational,
professional,orsocialcontent.

Antagonistic traits

Language further complicates bias analysis.
Gender bias varies substantially across languages,
shaped by grammatical gender systems and cultural
context (Rowe et al., 2025). Hindi, the world’s third
most spoken language (eth, 2025), encodes gender
through adjective agreement and verb morphol-
ogy rather than pronouns (Hall, 2016), and prior
work on Hindi shows gender bias interacts with

both representations and generation (Malik et al.,
2022; Gupta et al., 2025; Hada et al., 2024). Yet,
personality-conditioned narrative generation in
Hindiremainslargelyunexplored.
In this work, we investigate how personality
conditioning influences gender bias in persona-
driven LLM interactions. We conduct a large-scale
controlled study of persona-conditioned story
generation in English and Hindi.
We systemati-
cally vary persona gender, occupational role (see
Appendix A.2), and personality traits from the
HEXACO and Dark Triad frameworks, generating
23, 400 artifacts across six diverse Language Mod-
els(LMs). Toquantifygenderbiasintheseartifacts,
we introduce a sentence-level embedding-based
metric that measures semantic alignment with
male and female-stereotypical reference centroids,
enablingbiaslocalizationwithinartifacts(Caliskan
etal.,2017;Mayetal.,2019).
Weaddressthefollowingresearchquestions:
• RQ1:
Are personality traits associated
with different levels of gender bias in LLM-
generatedartifacts?
• RQ2: Do personality and gender interact to
amplifyorattenuategenderbias?
• RQ3: How do these interaction effects differ
acrosslanguages?
Our analysis reveals that gender bias in LLM-
generated narratives is not static, but strongly
context-dependent. Dark Triad traits consistently
amplify
gender-stereotypical
representations,
while prosocial traits tend to attenuate them. These
effects persist across models, occupations, and
languages, and in many cases exceed the influ-
ence of the explicit gender label itself.
We also
observe distinct patterns in Hindi compared to
English,reflectinginteractionsbetweenpersonality
conditioningandgrammaticalgendermarking.
Ourcontributionsare:
• A large multilingual corpus of personality-
conditionedartifactsspanninggender,occupa-
tion,andpsychologicaltraits.
• A sentence-level centroid-based metric for
quantifyinggenderbiasinartifactgeneration.
• Empirical evidence that personality traits act
as systematic bias amplifiers or attenuators in
LLMoutputs.
• Analysis across languages, occupations, and
model architectures, highlighting implica-

RelatedWork
2.1
GenderBiasesinLLMsandNarrative
Generation
Prior work has extensively shown that language
modelsencodegenderstereotypes,associatingmen
and women with different occupations, traits, and
social roles. Early embedding-based analyses and
benchmarkdatasets(e.g.,WEAT/SEAT,WinoBias,
StereoSet, CrowS-Pairs) demonstrate that such
biases persist across representations and down-
stream tasks (Caliskan et al., 2017; May et al., 2019;
Zhao et al., 2018; Nadeem et al., 2021; Nangiaet al.,
2020).
As LMs became more generative, studies shifted
toward narrative and discourse-level bias revealing
thatgenderbiasoftenmanifeststhroughdifferences
in agency, sentiment, and evaluative framing. Male
characters are portrayed as more agentic and author-
itative, while female characters are described us-
ing more communal or emotional language (Lucy
and Bamman, 2021; Wan et al., 2023; Masoudian
et al., 2025; Kong et al., 2024) with masculine de-
faults persisting even under gender-neutral prompts
(DoyenandTodirascu,2025;Telekietal.,2025).

Gender bias also varies across languages. Hindi
and other Indic languages remain underexplored
despite their large speaker populations (Rowe et al.,
2025; eth, 2025). Existing work shows that Hindi
gender bias interacts with grammatical gender,
occupation, and social hierarchy, and that English-
centric bias measures do not transfer directly to
gender-marking languages (Malik et al., 2022;
Gupta et al., 2025; Hada et al., 2024; Hall, 2016).
However, these studies do not consider persona- or
personality-conditionedgeneration.
2.2
PersonaConditioning,PersonalityTraits
andBiasModulation
Persona prompting significantly shapes LLM
behaviour, affecting tone, style, and content, and
prompt formulation itself can influence stereotyp-
ing (Lutz et al., 2025). LLMs have also been shown
to exhibit stable patterns along psychological
dimensions such as the Big Five, HEXACO, and
DarkTriad(Salechaetal.,2024;Zhengetal.,2025).
Critically, personality conditioning can modulate
harmful behaviours, including toxicity and bias,
with certain personality traits acting as amplifiers
and others as attenuators (Wang et al., 2025; Li
et al., 2024).
Persona-based prompts have also
been shown to elicit implicit reasoning biases even
when surface outputs appear neutral (Gupta et al.,
2024). However, this literature typically examines
personality or gender separately, without modeling
their interactions across occupational context or
language.
2.3
PositionofThisWork
Prior work establishes that LLMs exhibit gender
bias in narratives and that persona and personality
prompts shape model behaviour. What remains un-
explored is how personality traits modulate gender
bias through interaction effects, particularly in mul-
tilingual narrative generation grounded in occupa-
tionalcontexts.
Our work addresses this gap by systematically
varying gender, occupation, and HEXACO and
Dark Triad personality traits in English and Hindi
story generation.
Unlike prior studies, we exam-
ine personality–gender interactions and measure
story-levelbiasusingasentence-basedapproach.

Personas are assigned one of three gen-

Occupation.
To situate personas in realistic

2015).
Following prior work on occupational
gender stereotypes (Bolukbasi et al., 2016; Zhao

generation (e.g., design a lesson integrating group
work to enhance student collaboration ). See Ap-
pendixA.2formoredetails.
Language.
Since our occupational scenarios are
grounded in the Indian socio-cultural context, we

chopathy), yielding 9 distinct personality traits.

Measurement
We represent gender stereotypes in a shared embed-
ding space using male and female centroids derived
from gender-stereotypical language.
Intuitively,
the male centroid encodes traits such as being
”leader-like”, ”ambitious”, and ”assertive”, while
the female centroid encodes traits like ”nurturing”,
”empathetic”, ”cooperative”, and ”graceful” (Fast
et al., 2016; Bolukbasi et al., 2016). This enables us
toquantifyhowcloselyagivensentencealignswith
male- or female-coded stereotypes in both English
and Hindi. We construct the respective centroids in
threesteps.
Step 1: Stereotypical word lists:
We manually
compile gender-stereotypical word lists in English
following prior work on occupational and trait-
based gender bias (Fast et al., 2016; Hoyle et al.,
2019). Eachlist contains approximately 200 −210
items, covering nouns, verbs, and adjectives (e.g.,
engineer, decisive, dominates for male; caregiver,
empathetic, supports for female). We then translate
these words into Hindi and iteratively refine with
native speakers to ensure stereotypical validity in
Hindi usage.
We also check these words against
prior works (Malik et al., 2022; Kirtane and Anand,

DiscussionandConclusion
We presented a controlled study of persona-
conditioned story generation in English and
Hindi, varying persona gender, occupation, and
HEXACO and Dark Triad traits across 23,400
artifacts from six LLMs.
Using a sentence-level
centroid-based bias metric validated by human
annotation, we show that gender bias is context-
dependent rather than fixed:
Dark Triad traits
consistently
amplify
male-stereotypical
align-
ment, HEXACO traits have mixed effects, and
in some cases personality effects exceed those of
explicit gender labels. We also find that Hindi has
a stronger baseline male-stereotypical skew, while
personality-driven modulation is more pronounced
in English. Together, these results highlight person-
ality prompts as fairness-critical design parameters
inpersona-drivenmultilingualsystems.
These findings carry broader implications for
persona-driven LLM deployment.
If personal-
ity cues can systematically amplify or attenuate
gender-stereotypical language, then bias should
not be understood as a static model artifact, but as
an emergent property of the interaction between
model, prompt design, and linguistic context. In
practical applications such as educational sup-
port, workplace writing assistance, and customer
service,
persona specifications may therefore
act as fairness-critical controls that shape how
professions, competencies, and social roles are rep-
resented to users. The cross-linguistic differences
weobservefurthersuggestthatmitigationstrategies
cannot be assumed to transfer uniformly across
languages.
Future work could extend persona-conditioned
analysis beyond gender to other social categories
(e.g., caste, religion, disability), as well as to multi-
turn interactions in which personas evolve over
time, to support richer evaluations and provide
clearerguidanceforsaferpersonadesign.

Limitations
Our study focuses on a single task family, which
is,occupation-groundedartifactgenerationinanIn-

tions, which may limit generalization to other do-
mains or interaction styles. The personality frame-
works used (HEXACO and Dark Triad) originate
from Western personality psychology and may not
fully capture personality constructs across Indian
culturalcontexts.
Bias is measured using a centroid-based em-
bedding metric with manually curated stereotype
lexicons, making the results dependent on the
chosen encoder and lexical sets.
The stereotype
word lists, though refined with native speakers,
were originally compiled in English and translated
into Hindi, which may introduce translation arti-
facts or fail to capture Hindi-specific stereotypical
expressions that have no direct English equivalent.
Personality prompt validation via the SD3 test was
conductedonGPT-5nanoonly; thedegreetowhich
thesamepromptsreliablyelicittargetedpersonality
profiles in architecturally distinct models (e.g.,
Falcon-Mamba SSM, DeepSeek-R1 LRM) was not
independently verified. Methodologically, we treat
each generated story as an independent sample and
evaluate only six contemporary models, leaving
open how persona-driven bias may manifest in
longerconversationsorinnewerarchitectures.
Our bias metric aggregates to a single sentence-
level maximum score per story, which captures the
most salient stereotypical statement but discards in-
formation about the overall distributional tendency
of the artifact. Alternative aggregation strategies
(e.g., mean score, proportion of biased sentences)
may yield different conclusions. Furthermore, our
metric measures alignment with pre-defined stereo-
typical centroids and does not capture more sub-
tle or intersectional forms of bias, such as caste-
or class-based stereotyping that may co-occur with
genderinIndianoccupationalcontexts.
The human annotation study involved only three
annotators evaluating 100 story pairs, which, while
showing substantial inter-annotator agreement, rep-
resents a limited sample relative to the full corpus
of 23, 400 artifacts. Annotation was also limited
to pairwise comparisons against a neutral baseline,
and did not assess absolute stereotyping severity or
capture annotator demographic variation that may
influencestereotypeperception.
Finally, our controlled prompts simulate persona
effects but do not reflect real-world chatbot usage
patterns or user query distributions.
Personality
conditioning in deployment settings is rarely as ex-
plicitorstructuredasourprompts,andusersmayin-
duce similar effects through more subtle cues. We
also do not measure real-world consequences using
live user data, nor do we investigate whether simi-
lar patterns arise in other languages or cultural con-
texts.

Our study conditions language models on Dark

ModelSelectionRationale
To ensure that our findings are not specific to a
single model architecture, we evaluate a diverse
set of contemporary language models spanning
different design paradigms and capability levels.
The selected models, that are, GPT-5 nano, Llama-
3.3-70B-Instruct, Gemma-3-1B-it, DeepSeek-R1,
Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct,
and Falcon-Mamba-7B-
Instruct represent different architectural families,
including standard transformer-based LLMs, small
language
models,
reasoning-oriented
models,
mixture-of-experts architectures, and state-space
models.
This diversity allows us to examine
whether personality-conditioned gender bias pat-
terns generalize across fundamentally different
model designs rather than being an artifact of a
specific architecture.
We include models with
different parameter sizes and training objectives to
assess whether the interaction between personality
conditioning and gender bias is consistent across
models with different capacities and inductive
biases.
ChoiceofSentenceEmbeddingModel
Our bias metric relies on sentence embeddings to
measure semantic similarity between generated ar-
tifacts and gender-stereotypical reference centroids.
Since our study focuses on Hindi and Indian occu-
pational contexts, we use IndicSBERT, a multilin-
gualsentenceencodertrainedspecificallyonalarge
collection of Indian languages. IndicSBERT has
beenshowntobettercapturesemanticrelationships
in Indian languages compared to general-purpose
multilingualencoders(Deodeetal.,2023).
We also experimented with LaBSE, a widely
used multilingual sentence embedding model
(Feng et al., 2022). However, preliminary experi-
ments indicated that LaBSE produced less distinct
separation between male- and female-aligned sim-
ilarity distributions across personality conditions.
In contrast, IndicSBERT yielded clearer and more
stable bias patterns, hence, we use IndicSBERT
as the primary encoder in our bias computation
pipeline.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increas- ingly deployed in persona-driven applications such as education, customer service, and social platforms, where models are prompted to adopt specific personas when interacting with users. While persona conditioning can improve user experience and engagement, it also raises con- cerns about how personality cues may interact with gender biases and stereotypes. In this work, we present a controlled study of persona- conditioned story generation in English and Hindi, where each story portrays a working pro- fessional in India producing context-specific artifacts (e.g., lesson plans, reports, letters) under systematically varied persona gender, oc- cupational role, and personality traits from the HEXACO and Dark Triad frameworks. Across 23, 400 generated stories from six state-of-the- art LLMs, we find that personality traits are significantly associated with both the magni- tude and direction of gender bias. In particular, Dark Triad personality traits are consistently associated with higher gender-stereotypical representations compared to socially desirable HEXACO traits, though these associations vary across models and languages. Our find- ings demonstrate that gender bias in LLMs is not static but context-dependent. This suggests that persona-conditioned systems used in real-world applications may introduce uneven representational harms, reinforcing gender stereotypes in generated educational, professional,orsocialcontent.
